read.sections.0.heading.back: A place and a turning point
read.sections.0.heading.source: A place and a turning point

read.sections.0.text.back: On 15 February 1942, British forces surrendered to Japanese forces at the Ford Factory in Singapore. This was the start of the Japanese occupation, which lasted until 1945. Now the factory holds an exhibition about the war, run by the Singapore National Archives. During the occupation, daily activities changed. Many schools closed or were used for other things, and many children lost time learning in class. Not everyone went through the same events in the same way. A photo of the building now can show us a place. That photo cannot show how people lived there in 1942.
read.sections.0.text.source: On 15 February 1942, British forces surrendered to Japanese forces at the Ford Factory in Singapore. This began the Japanese occupation, which lasted until 1945. Today the factory holds an exhibition about the war, run by the National Archives of Singapore. During the occupation, everyday routines changed. Many schools closed or were used for other things, and many children lost time in class. People did not all live through the same events in the same way. A photo of the building today can show us a place. It cannot show us how people lived there in 1942.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: On 15 February 1942, British forces handed over Singapore. Japanese forces took over. This was the start of the Japanese occupation. This occupation lasted until 1945. The British surrendered in a factory. Now that building holds an exhibition about the war. Daily life changed in this time. Many schools closed. Many children could not go to school. Each person's life was different. A photo of the building now shows a place. That photo does not show the way people lived in 1942.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: On 15 February 1942, British forces gave up Singapore. Japanese forces took control. This was the start of the Japanese occupation. It lasted until 1945. The British gave up in a factory. Today the building has a show about the war. Daily life changed in this time. Many schools closed. Many children missed school. People had different lives. A photo of the building today shows a place. It does not show how people lived in 1942.

read.sections.1.text.back: The MOE Heritage Centre, the education history centre of Singapore's Ministry of Education, writes about school in this time. According to that history centre, the Japanese military government made Japanese-language lessons compulsory in schools in 1942. Teachers had to learn Japanese, and they were not allowed to use English at school. There was a shortage of food, so many schools grew their own food. Gardening became part of lessons. Cassava, a root plant that grows easily, became an important food. This source tells about rules and examples of school life. This source does not say that every child went to school or got the same lessons. For most children, school almost stopped.

This source tells us about rules and examples of school life. It does not tell us that every child went to school or had the same lessons. For most children, school almost stopped.

read.sections.2.heading.back: Food and the limit of a source

read.sections.2.text.note: Indonesian "nasi" (cooked rice) is used for "instead of rice" (what people ate) and "beras" (uncooked rice) for the ration and the ships.
read.sections.2.text.back: Before the war, Singapore bought most of its food from other places. The war cut off the ships and trains that brought rice. In 2019, Lee Geok Boi wrote about food in wartime for Singapore's National Library. She used oral history interviews. She explains that every home needed a ration card, and the rice ration got smaller over time. Many people ate cassava and sweet potatoes in place of rice. Some food was sold secretly at a very high price, so people who had more money could get more food. For most people, their food was not enough to stay healthy. To know about people's food at that time, we need records about food or people's memories, not a photo of the factory now.
read.sections.2.text.source: Before the war, Singapore bought most of its food from other places. The war cut the ships and trains that brought rice. Lee Geok Boi wrote about wartime food for the National Library in 2019. She used oral history interviews. She explains that every home needed a ration card, and the rice ration got smaller over time. Many people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes instead of rice. Some food was sold in secret at very high prices, so people with more money could get more. For most people, meals were not enough to stay healthy. To learn about meals then, we need food records or memories, not a photo of the factory now.

read.sections.2.simpler.back: Before the war, most food came to Singapore by ship. The war stopped many rice shipments. Lee Geok Boi wrote about this in 2019. She used oral history. Every home needed a ration card. Over time, the rice ration got smaller. Many people ate cassava and sweet potatoes. Some food was sold secretly, at a high price. Most people did not get enough food to stay healthy. The photo of the factory does not show what people ate.

watch.summary.back: This video is part of a cooking show from Singapore's National Library. A librarian and a guest cook, Lee Geok Boi, make food from the time of the Japanese occupation. First, they talk about the past. There was a shortage of rice in wartime. So people ate cassava and sweet potatoes instead. Cassava is easy to grow. This video also talks about rations, and about food that was sold secretly at a high price. Then Lee Geok Boi cooks two dishes. She only uses ingredients people could get at that time. She makes noodles from cassava and sweet potato. She also makes boiled cassava with coconut. The video says that cassava fills you up, but does not give the body everything it needs to stay healthy.
watch.summary.source: This video is part of a cooking show from Singapore's National Library. A librarian and a guest cook, Lee Geok Boi, make food from the time of the Japanese occupation. First, they talk about the past. There was a shortage of rice in the war. So people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes instead. Tapioca was easy to grow. The video also talks about rations, and about food that was sold in secret for a lot of money. Then Lee Geok Boi cooks two dishes. She uses only foods that people could get at the time. She makes noodles from tapioca and sweet potato. She also makes boiled tapioca with coconut. The video says tapioca fills you up, but it does not give the body all it needs to stay healthy.

"Displacement" became "harus meninggalkan rumah" (had to leave home), plain and non-technical. "Many people were harmed" became "banyak orang menjadi korban" (many people became victims).
sensitiveNotes.0.back: This lesson is about an occupation in wartime, and some learners have been through war, conflict or had to leave home. Never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war or of having to leave home, or about their home country, religion or ethnic group, and never ask them to compare their lives with the people in the sources. Keep the discussion on the sources about school and food, and allow any learner to leave the discussion without giving a reason. This lesson needs no images of violence. The occupation also brought killings and cruel punishments; this lesson does not explain them and the educator does not need to explain them either. If learners bring them up, say clearly that many people became victims, then go back to the sources. Check first before sharing: the NLB article mentions a cruel punishment in one line, and this video may show photos of starving prisoners of war (from 5:04).
sensitiveNotes.0.source: This lesson is about a wartime occupation, and some learners have lived through war, conflict or displacement. Never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war or displacement, or about their home country, religion or ethnicity, and never ask them to compare their lives with the people in the sources. Keep the discussion on the sources about school and food, and let any learner step out without giving a reason. The lesson needs no violent images. The occupation also brought killings and harsh punishments; the lesson does not describe them and you do not need to. If learners raise them, say plainly that many people were harmed, then return to the sources. Preview before sharing: the NLB article mentions a harsh punishment in one line, and the video may show photos of starving prisoners of war (from 5:04).

educatorNotes.0.back: Aim: learners explain two different changes in daily life, one about school and one about food, with one source for each, without saying that everyone lived the same way. Step for reading evidence: compare the school rules from the MOE Heritage Centre with Lee Geok Boi's food history, then point to the photo's date, 2025, before learners say what the photo shows. A good answer names two different everyday effects supported by sources. Misunderstandings to straighten out: "all children still went to school as usual", "everyone ate the same food", and the idea that the occupation by itself brought independence later.

educatorNotes.1.back: Notes on the sources: the MOE page records rules and examples, not the situation of every school. The NLB article uses oral history interviews from the National Archives (its first Japanese Occupation project, 1981–1985, recorded 179 people); memories are valuable, but each memory is one person's story, told decades later. This lesson on purpose does not include the ration amounts and prices from that article. The photo shows the restored building in 2025 with modern flats behind it. If a licensed photo of a wartime ration card with a clear origin can be found, that photo would make a stronger second picture.
